newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: FOCUS - Cement giant Holderbank slashes profits.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Cement giant Holderbank slashes profits.

text.p: Holderbank, the world's biggest cement maker, on Tuesday slashed 1996 net profits with surprise provisions totalling 607 million Swiss francs ($413.2 million) for cutting capacity in sated markets.
Analysts welcomed the unexpected move as raising profit potential by cutting costs in the sluggish and oversupplied West European cement market.

"I welcome this move...There is no reason the share price should fall tommorrow (Wednesday)," UBS analyst Remo Rosenau said after Holderbank realeased its statement following the Swiss stock exchange close.
Bearer shares in Holderbank Financiere Glarus AG, the group's full name, closed before the 1996 results statement at 1,137 Swiss francs, nine francs up on the prior close.
Holderbank said the extraordinary provisions and value adjusments totalling 607 million would burden the bottom line by 450 million Swiss francs after taxes.
Net profit before minority interests and extraordinaries was 646 million Swiss francs, up from 611 million the year before, revised due to a switch to International Accounting Standards (IAS).

After minority interests that are traditionally large due to Holderbank's many cement and materials ventures, net profit attributable to shareholders would have been 493 million after 450 million in 1995.
But after the extraordinary provisions, net profit fopr Holderbank sharehodlers was just 43 million Swiss banks.
Holderbank said its board proposed an unchanged dividend of 17 Swiss francs per bearer and 3.40 per registered share.
Holderbank, which makes cement, concrete, clinker and aggregates for world markets, said the extraordinary provisions were the cost of scaling down capacity and covering heightened business risk.
"The specific provisions and valuation adjustments are an extension of the restructurings already announced for switzerland, Germany, France, Canada and Australia," it said.
The European cement market in particular was saturated at a low level after earlier boom years, it said.
The measures and special provisions would allow fixed costs to be cut by a sustainable 50 million Swiss francs a year, Holderbank said.

UBS's Rosenau said there was significant cost cutting potential in Europe, where a thick network of Holderbank plants had a low capacity usage of around 75 percent. He had raised Holderbank to a "buy" in a January study.
"Taking such a big, single step with these provisions was a surprise...This frees up profit potential that will have some effects this year, more in 1998 and full effects in 1999," he told Reuters.
"To ensure cost leadership pursuant to our strategy, structurally induced capacity reduction is required," Holderbank said.

But Holderbank said it would still be able to serve European markets optimally even after shrinking capacity because of a "uniquely dense network of production locations", both wholly owned and through minorities in several European companies.
In Switzerland, Holderbank said subsidiary HCB would close its Rekingen cement plant at the start of 1998, one of five Swiss cement factories run by the group.

Based in the central Swiss town of Glarus, Holderbank sold 53.5 million tonnes of cement and clinker in 1995. It has invested heavily in recent years in expanding production in growing markets in Latin America and Asia to escape a downturn in its largest markets in Europe. ($ = 1.468 Swiss Francs)
